facts: The paper is titled "Understanding and Improving Information Preservation in Prompt Compression for LLMs."
Weronika Łajewska is affiliated with the University of Stavanger.
The research investigates prompt compression techniques in large language models.
The authors aim to improve the integrity and utility of prompts during compression.
Recent advancements in large language models have led to their application in various tasks.
Prompt compression techniques have been developed to balance input length and performance.
Improvements of up to 23% in downstream performance were achieved through refined soft prompting.
The optimal trade-off was found with soft prompting combined with sequence-level training.
Recent advancements in large language models have enabled their application to tasks requiring long-context input.
Soft methods of prompt compression allow for higher compression rates but are less interpretable than hard methods.
The framework proposed evaluates hard-prompting method LLMLingua and soft-prompting methods xRAG and PISCO.
PISCO achieves the best balance between compression and effectiveness among the evaluated methods.
Prompt compression enhances the efficiency of large language models (LLMs) by creating smaller, approximate representations of prompts.
Hard prompting focuses on producing concise text versions while retaining key information.
Notable soft prompting approaches include AutoCompressors, Gisting, ICAE, 500xCompressor, and xRAG.
Evaluation of these methods typically involves downstream tasks such as classification and QA.
The benchmarking of prompt compression methods focuses on limited tasks like text classification and extractive QA/RC.
Examples of text classification tasks mentioned are MNLI and SuperGLUE.
The authors advocate for including generation tasks in the evaluation of prompt compression methods.
They suggest that evaluation criteria should evolve with advancements in compression methods and large language models.
The evaluation of compression quality is based on three key dimensions: downstream task performance, grounding, and information preservation.
BERTScore (F1) is used for summarization in evaluating downstream task performance.
FABLES is selected for grounding due to its alignment with human evaluation.
The framework monitors compression rates, reflecting the size ratio of compressed to original prompts.
The analysis focuses on four prompt compression methods using the Mistral-7B Instruct v0.2 LLM.
xRAG encodes input text as a single token through an encoder model and a trainable modality bridge.
PISCO enhances xRAG by incorporating an encoder adapter and a decoder adapter.
LLMLingua utilizes a token-level iterative pruning algorithm to maintain semantic integrity.

The Mistral-7B model experiences performance drops ranging from 3% to 55% when context is fully removed. The most substantial performance decline for the Mistral-7B model is observed in HotpotQA. In long document summarization, the difference between base Mistral and compression methods is a minimal 4% relative difference. PISCO shows improvements on HotpotQA, suggesting benefits from refining models to capture finer details.
The xRAG method results in a 30-point decrease in groundedness scores on HotpotQA.
The xRAG method leads to a 50-point decrease in groundedness scores on QuAC.
LLMLingua shows reduced hallucinations compared to other methods.
PISCO achieves the highest fidelity in responses despite high compression.
xRAG has an average BERTScore F1 of 0.66.
xRAG shows a significant drop in reconstruction quality when using one token per sentence.
PISCO maintains a higher encoding capacity with 8 embeddings compared to xRAG's single token compression.
xRAG requires 3.7x10^7 MFLOPs for its computational costs.
The section evaluates the computational efficiency of various prompt compression methods.
The HotpotQA dataset is used to measure the floating-point operations (FLOPs) needed for compression.
The xRAG method has limitations in retaining detailed information in long-context scenarios.
The authors plan to re-train an xRAG model referred to as xRAG (Reproduced).
The xRAG model uses a bridge model to align embedding spaces from a dense retrieval encoder and a target LLM.
Single-sentence samples are utilized in the pre-training of the xRAG model.
The variant xRAG w/ Sentence PT + FT shows significant performance improvements across various tasks.
The model preserves only 13%-39% of entities on average when using sentence-level compression.
The approach is called xRAG w/ Two-Step PT + FT.
There is a 23% relative improvement in downstream tasks.
The model reconstructs 50% of entities from multi-token encoded texts.
The baseline reconstructs only 13% of entities from multi-token encoded texts.
The qualitative analysis involved 10 samples generated from 20 prompts.
xRAG tokens primarily capture the general topic of the content.
The language model effectively reconstructs main entities related to the TriviaQA dataset.
Numerical entities like dates and numbers are frequently lost by the model.
PISCO is the leading method for prompt compression in long-context scenarios.
The sentence-level xRAG achieves a 4x-12x reduction in input size.
The sentence-level xRAG has a 2x higher compression rate compared to LLMLingua.
The compression rate varies with input lengths in the described methods.
Many methods, such as xRAG, struggle to preserve essential details like numbers and names.
Proposed modifications to xRAG aim to improve information retention and grounding.
The introduction of multi-token context understanding through PISCO shows promise in enhancing compression techniques.
The text advocates for a hybrid approach that combines hard and soft prompting to minimize information loss during compression.
The paper evaluates the quality of prompt compression methods in long-context generation tasks.
The study highlights the strengths and weaknesses of hard compression (LLMLingua) and soft compression (xRAG and PISCO).
The proposed improvements to the xRAG method resulted in a 23% increase in downstream task performance.
The code repository for this research is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/information-preservation-in-prompt-compression.
The study emphasizes the need for future research to explore different model sizes and architectures.
The analysis is restricted to one representative baseline from each category of prompt compression techniques.
The appendix details the implementation and experimental setup for training the xRAG model with the Mistral-7B Instruct v0.2 LLM.
Mistral-7B achieved the highest grounding scores, but challenges in entity preservation and information hallucination were prevalent.
